lessons.title: What Is No-Code?
objectives: Describe what a no-code builder actually does, and name the kinds of app it builds well and the kinds it builds badly
State the three permanent costs of no-code - the subscription, the lock-in and the ceiling - before choosing it for a project
Explain why data modelling, not drag-and-drop, is the skill that decides whether a no-code app works
lessons.notes:
A no-code builder is a visual editor that creates an application for you over a database you define. You arrange screens, describe where data comes from, and set what buttons do. The platform generates and runs the app.

What it removes is the typing of code and the running of servers. What it does not remove is the thinking: deciding what your data looks like, who is allowed to see which parts of it, and what the app is actually for. Those are the hard parts, and they are identical whether you write code or not.

WHAT NO-CODE GENUINELY DOES WELL

- INTERNAL TOOLS. A stock list for a shop, a delivery tracker, a maintenance log, a field-visit form. These are small, used by a known handful of people, and would never justify a developer's fee. This is where no-code is strongest and where most of the paid work is.
- DIRECTORIES AND CATALOGUES. A list of members, suppliers, properties, service providers, with search and filters.
- BOOKINGS AND REQUESTS. Appointments, room bookings, service requests, approval flows.
- DATA COLLECTION IN THE FIELD. Forms that work on a phone, replacing paper.
- PROVING AN IDEA. A rough first version to put in front of ten real users before anybody spends money building properly.

WHAT IT DOES BADLY, AND YOU SHOULD NOT FIGHT IT

- HEAVY COMPUTATION. Anything doing real processing on large volumes.
- COMPLEX CUSTOM LOGIC. Rules with many branches and exceptions become an unreadable tangle of visual blocks that nobody, including you in three months, can follow.
- STRICT PERFORMANCE DEMANDS. You do not control how the generated app fetches data, so you cannot optimise your way out of slowness.
- GENUINELY OFFLINE-FIRST USE. Some platforms cache; few handle long periods offline with conflicting edits well. If your users work where there is no network for hours, test this before promising it.
- ANYTHING THAT MUST BE CHEAP AT LARGE SCALE. Pricing usually rises with users, rows or apps. The thing that is cheap at twenty users can be unaffordable at two thousand.

THE THREE PERMANENT COSTS

Name these out loud before you choose a platform, because all three are discovered late by people who did not.

1. THE SUBSCRIPTION NEVER ENDS. A no-code app is not a thing you build and own; it is a thing you rent while it runs. Stop paying and it stops working. The monthly fee is usually in dollars, charged to a card, and it rises when you cross a tier. Over three years the subscription often exceeds what the build was worth.

2. LOCK-IN IS REAL. In most cases you cannot export a working application. You can usually export your DATA as a spreadsheet or a dump, and you should check that you can before committing. But the app itself - the screens, the logic - lives in that vendor's account and cannot be moved to another. If the vendor raises prices, changes direction or closes, your options are narrow. One category of tool is different, and lesson 5 covers it.

3. THE CEILING ARRIVES WITHOUT WARNING. Every platform has limits: rows per app, file storage, how many screens, what its logic blocks can express, how fast a long list loads. You will not meet them on day one. You meet them when the app is live and people depend on it, which is the worst moment to discover the platform cannot do the next thing you need.

So the question to ask before building is not "can this tool do what I need today". It is "what is the next thing I will need, and can it do that too".

THE KENYAN REALITIES THAT CHANGE THE DECISION

- PAYING FOR IT. Subscriptions are in dollars and need a card enabled for international payments. Your client probably cannot pay the vendor by M-Pesa. Lesson 6 deals with who holds that subscription, and the answer matters more than it sounds.
- YOUR USERS' PHONES. Most will open the app on a mid-range or older Android phone, on metered data, on a connection that varies. A builder's preview on a laptop over fibre tells you nothing about that. Test on a cheap phone, on mobile data, before you show anybody.
- APP SIZE AND DATA USE. A heavy app that downloads large images every time it opens costs your users money to use. That is a design constraint, not a detail.
- WHAT PEOPLE WILL ACTUALLY PAY FOR. Kenyan small businesses, schools, clinics, churches, cooperatives and NGOs have real, unmet need for simple internal data tools. That is a market. A consumer app competing with established free apps is a much harder sell.

THE SKILL THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS: DATA MODELLING

Here is the thing nobody tells beginners. Most no-code projects that fail do not fail because the builder could not do something. They fail because the data was structured wrongly at the start, and every screen built on top of it then fought the structure.

Data modelling means deciding, before you touch a screen:

- WHAT ARE THE THINGS? Each type of thing gets its own table: customers, orders, products, visits.
- ONE ROW IS ONE THING. One customer per row. One order per row. If a row holds three orders in three columns, you have already lost.
- HOW DO THEY RELATE? An order belongs to one customer; a customer has many orders. Write those sentences down; they become your relationships.
- WHAT MUST NEVER BE REPEATED? If a customer's phone number is typed into every order, then changing it means changing it everywhere, and it will be wrong in some of them. Store it once, in the customer row, and point at it.

Get that right on paper and the app almost builds itself. Get it wrong and no amount of drag-and-drop will save it - you will rebuild.

HOW TO DECIDE WHETHER TO USE NO-CODE AT ALL

Use it when the app is small to medium, the users are countable, the logic is simple, speed of delivery matters more than control, and somebody will keep paying the subscription.

Do not use it when the app is the core of a business that must survive a vendor's decisions, when the logic is genuinely complex, or when the economics only work if the running cost is near zero at scale.

And there is an honest third answer that gets forgotten: sometimes the right tool is a well-built spreadsheet with a form attached. If a shared sheet and a form solve the problem, that is not a failure of ambition; it is the cheapest correct answer, and it has no subscription at all.
lessons.practice:
Decide whether no-code fits your project, then do the part that actually decides success.

Step 1. Write the project in one sentence: who uses it, what they do with it, and what problem disappears when it works.

Step 2. Score it against the fit list. Write yes or no to each:

- Fewer than about fifty regular users?
- Logic simple enough to describe in five sentences?
- No heavy computation?
- Works acceptably with an internet connection present?
- Somebody identified who will pay the monthly subscription?

If you wrote no to two or more, write one sentence on whether a spreadsheet with a form, or a coded application, is the better answer.

Step 3. Price the three-year subscription. Find a candidate platform's published monthly price for the tier you would actually need, multiply by 36, and convert to shillings. Write that figure. Then write what the build itself is worth. Compare them.

Step 4. Check the exit before the entrance. On your candidate platform's documentation, find and write down: can you export your data, in what format, and can you export the app itself? If you cannot find the answer, that is the answer.

Step 5. Now model the data on paper, before opening any tool.

- List the THINGS. One line each.
- For each thing, list its fields.
- Write the relationships as plain sentences: "an order belongs to one customer", "a customer has many orders".
- Find anything repeated across rows and move it to its own table.

Step 6. Test your model against three real questions the app must answer, for example "which customers ordered last month" or "how much stock is left of item X". If answering one of them needs data your model does not hold, fix the model now. This step prevents the commonest rebuild.

Step 7. Write your device constraint in one line: the cheapest phone and the slowest connection your app must work on. You will test against this in the lessons that follow, and it is the test most beginners skip.

quiz.question: What is the most common reason a no-code project has to be rebuilt?
options: The builder lacked a visual feature the project needed
The data was structured wrongly at the start, so every screen fought the structure
The subscription was too expensive
The app was not published to an app store

quiz.question: A client asks you to build their core business application in a no-code tool. What is the most important thing to tell them first?
options: That it will look less professional than coded software
That it stops working if the subscription lapses, and the app itself usually cannot be moved to another platform
That no-code apps cannot store customer data
That it will be finished faster, so the price should be lower

lessons.title: Comparing the Tools
objectives: Pick a platform from the shape of the project rather than from a review, using four questions that eliminate most options immediately
Read a pricing model for the trap it hides - per user, per app, per row, or per published app
Judge lock-in by asking what you can get out, and know which category of tool avoids it
lessons.notes:
There are hundreds of no-code platforms and comparison articles are mostly useless, because they list features rather than asking what you are building. Four questions eliminate nearly all of them in ten minutes.

QUESTION 1: WHAT SHAPE IS THE THING?

- A DATA APP FOR A SMALL KNOWN GROUP - stock, visits, bookings, approvals. Spreadsheet-backed builders are strongest here: fastest to build, cheapest, and your client can already read the data because it is a sheet.
- A CONSUMER MOBILE APP that needs to be in the app stores with its own look. You need a builder that produces installable apps, which means a steeper tool and the app-store process in lesson 4.
- A WEBSITE WITH FORMS AND A DATABASE BEHIND IT. Web app builders and modern site builders with database features.
- A MARKETPLACE OR TWO-SIDED PLATFORM with payments. The hardest case. Possible, but this is where you meet the ceiling fastest, and payments plus personal data raise obligations you must handle properly.

QUESTION 2: WHO ARE THE USERS, AND HOW MANY?

- A handful of staff who log in: almost anything works, and per-user pricing will decide it.
- Hundreds or thousands of members of the public: row limits, performance on long lists and pricing at scale decide it.
- Anonymous visitors who do not log in: much simpler, and much cheaper.

QUESTION 3: DOES IT HAVE TO BE IN AN APP STORE?

Be honest, because this question carries real cost and delay. Most internal tools do NOT need to be in a store - a web app the user saves to their home screen looks and behaves close enough, installs instantly and updates without review.

If it genuinely must be in a store, you take on developer-account fees, a review process that can reject you, and a release cycle for every change. Lesson 4 covers that in detail.

QUESTION 4: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU WANT TO LEAVE?

Ask it now, not in year two. Three answers exist:

- DATA OUT ONLY. You can export rows; the app cannot move. Most spreadsheet-backed and app-store-style builders are here.
- DATA OUT, AND THE BACKEND IS ALREADY YOURS. Some builders sit on top of a database you own and control separately. If the vendor disappears, your data is untouched and a developer can build a new front end against it. This is a meaningful middle ground.
- CODE OUT. A small category of tool generates real source code you can export and have a developer continue. This is the only true escape hatch, and it is the subject of lesson 5.

Pick the weakest acceptable answer deliberately. Full lock-in is fine for a six-month internal tool and a bad idea for something a business will depend on for five years.

THE PRICING MODELS, AND THE TRAP IN EACH

Read the pricing page as carefully as the feature list. The model matters more than the headline number.

- PER EDITOR OR PER USER, PER MONTH. Fine for a tool with three staff. Ruinous for one with eighty, because the cost scales with exactly the thing you want to grow. Check whether it charges per person who USES the app or only per person who EDITS it; the difference is enormous.
- PER APP, PER MONTH. Predictable, and painful if you build five small apps for one client. Look for whether several apps can share one plan.
- PER ROW OR PER RECORD. Common on spreadsheet-backed tools. Looks generous until a form collects a few thousand submissions. Find the row limit of the tier you would buy and divide by your expected monthly submissions; that is how many months before you must upgrade.
- PER PUBLISHED APP PLUS STORE FEES. Add the annual and one-off store developer fees to the monthly price before comparing.
- FREE TIERS. Almost always carry a visible limit and an invisible one: the vendor's branding on your app, which a paying client will notice, and a cap on rows or users that arrives quietly.

Three more things that belong in the comparison and are usually left out:

- WHETHER IT CAN CONNECT TO ANYTHING ELSE. Can it call an external service, receive data, send an email, trigger a payment? A tool that cannot reach outside itself will block you eventually.
- HOW PERMISSIONS WORK. Can you make a row visible only to the user it belongs to? If the honest answer is no, the tool cannot hold anything private, which rules it out for most real work. Test this specifically; it is the commonest serious oversight.
- HOW IT BEHAVES ON A SLOW PHONE. Build the same small test app in your two finalists and open both on a cheap Android phone on mobile data. This ten-minute test overrules every review you will read.

A SENSIBLE DEFAULT FOR SOMEBODY STARTING

Learn ONE spreadsheet-backed builder properly, to the point where you can take a client's messy sheet and produce a working internal tool in a day. That skill is sellable immediately, the subscription is modest, and the data stays somewhere the client can read.

Then add ONE code-exporting builder later, for the projects that must go to a store or must survive a vendor. Two tools, learned properly, beat eight learned shallowly - and clients hire the person who can finish, not the person with the longest tool list.

AND THE OPTION THAT IS NOT A PLATFORM

Before you subscribe to anything: can this be a spreadsheet plus a form? No monthly fee, no lock-in, the client already understands it, and it can be handed over completely. For a surprising share of requests this is the correct answer, and recommending it when it is true is what makes a client trust the times you say they need more.
lessons.practice:
Choose a platform on evidence and prove the choice with a ten-minute test.

Step 1. Answer the four questions in writing for your project: what shape, how many users and whether they log in, app store or not, and the weakest acceptable exit. One line each.

Step 2. Shortlist exactly two platforms that fit those answers. Write the reason each one is on the list.

Step 3. For each, fill in this grid from the vendor's own pricing and documentation pages:

- Pricing model: per user, per app, per row, or other
- Monthly cost of the tier you would actually need
- The limit you would hit first, and the number
- Does the free tier put the vendor's branding on your app?
- Can a row be made visible only to the user it belongs to?
- Can it call an external service or send data out?
- What you can export: data only, data with your own backend, or source code

Step 4. Do the arithmetic that decides it. Take your expected number of users or monthly rows and work out which tier you need in month one and in month twelve. Write both monthly costs in shillings.

Step 5. Build the same tiny test app in both: one table, one list screen, one detail screen, one form. Time yourself in each.

Step 6. Run the test that overrules the reviews. Open both test apps on the cheapest Android phone you can borrow, on mobile data, not wifi. Write down for each: seconds to first useful screen, whether the list scrolled smoothly, and roughly how much data opening it used.

Step 7. Choose one. Write three sentences: which you chose, which single grid line decided it, and what you will do when you hit the limit you identified in step 3.

Step 8. Before you finish, write one honest line: could this project be a spreadsheet and a form instead? If yes, say why you are still choosing a platform.

quiz.question: A client wants an internal tool for eighty field staff who will each log in daily. Which pricing model is the biggest risk?
options: Per app, per month
Per user, per month, charged for everyone who uses the app
A one-off purchase price
Per row, with a high row limit

quiz.question: Two platforms both do what your project needs today. What is the most useful tie-breaker?
options: Which has more templates
Which has a nicer editor
What you can get out of each - data only, data on a backend you own, or exportable source code - and how each behaves on a cheap phone on mobile data
Which is more popular in reviews

lessons.title: Building an App in Glide
objectives: Build a spreadsheet-backed app by getting the table right first, so that screens become views of rows rather than hand-arranged pages
Make data private correctly using row owners and roles, instead of assuming a login hides anything
Work within row limits, computed columns and offline behaviour, and test the result on a cheap phone on mobile data
lessons.notes:
A spreadsheet-backed builder turns a table into an app. Each row becomes an item, each column becomes a field, and each screen is a view of some rows. Once that sentence is genuinely in your head, building is fast. Until it is, you will fight the tool.

THE TABLE IS THE APP

Start in the data, not the design. Set up your tables the way lesson 1 described: one row is one thing, each type of thing has its own table, nothing important repeated.

Then two habits that save whole rebuilds:

- GIVE EVERY ROW A STABLE UNIQUE ID, and never use the person's name or the product title as the identifier. Names change and repeat.
- DO NOT STORE A CALCULATION. If total equals quantity times price, compute it rather than typing it, so it cannot go stale or disagree with itself.

RELATIONS AND LOOKUPS, THE TWO CONCEPTS THAT UNLOCK EVERYTHING

Almost every real app needs one table to point at another: an order to its customer, a visit to its clinic, a payment to its invoice.

- A RELATION links rows in one table to matching rows in another, using a value they share. One order points to one customer; one customer points to many orders.
- A LOOKUP then pulls a field across that relation, so an order screen can show the customer's phone number without storing a copy of it.
- A ROLLUP summarises across a relation: the number of orders a customer has, the sum of their payments, the date of their last visit.

Those three cover most of what beginners try to achieve by copying data between sheets. Copying is the wrong instinct; it creates two versions of one truth and they will diverge.

COMPUTED COLUMNS, AND WHERE THEY RUN

Computed columns derive values without you editing data: templates that join text, maths columns, if-then columns, columns that extract part of a value.

One thing to understand about many of these: they are computed on the DEVICE, not in the sheet. That has two consequences. The computed value is not written back into your spreadsheet, so anything outside the app cannot see it. And a large table with many computed columns makes the app slower on a weak phone, because the work happens there.

THE PRIVACY MISTAKE THAT MATTERS MOST

This is the part beginners get wrong, and it is the one with real consequences.

A login screen does NOT make data private. By default, in this style of builder, the app downloads the data it needs to the device and then shows the user a filtered view. A filter is a display choice, not a security boundary. Filter a list to show only my orders and the other rows may still have reached my device.

What actually makes data private is ROW OWNERSHIP. You mark a column - usually the email address of the person the row belongs to - as the owner column, and the platform then sends only that person's rows to their device. Rows that are not yours never arrive.

So:

- Mark an owner column on any table holding personal, financial or confidential data. Do this before you put real data in, not after.
- Use ROLES for different kinds of user - staff, supervisor, member - and show or hide screens by role. Roles come from a column in your users table.
- Then TEST IT from a second account. Sign in as a different user and confirm you cannot see the first user's rows. Do not trust the editor's preview for this; test with real separate accounts.
- Remember that whoever can open the underlying spreadsheet can see everything regardless. Who has access to that sheet is part of your security model.

If the app will hold personal data about people in Kenya - names, phone numbers, health or financial details - you are handling personal data under the Data Protection Act 2019, with obligations about consent, purpose, retention and who can see it. Confirm the current requirements with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner rather than assuming a small app is exempt.

ROW LIMITS, AND THE PART PEOPLE DISCOVER TOO LATE

These platforms price by rows, and every tier has a ceiling. Two things to know:

- Find the exact limit of the tier you are on and divide it by your expected monthly new rows. That is how many months you have. Write the date in your calendar.
- Find out from the documentation what HAPPENS at the limit - whether new rows are rejected, whether the app stops updating, or whether you are simply billed more. These differ, and the difference matters if a form stops accepting submissions during a campaign.

Keep the table narrow and short on purpose: archive old rows to a separate table, do not store large images in the sheet when a link will do, and delete test data before launch.

OFFLINE, AND WHAT IT REALLY MEANS

These apps usually cache the data they have already loaded, so a user who opens the app with a connection can keep reading it briefly without one. That is not the same as working offline for a day and syncing later.

If your users are in the field with no signal for hours, test the exact scenario before promising anything: open the app offline from cold, add a record, close the app, come back online, and see whether the record arrives and what happens if somebody else changed the same row meanwhile. Whatever you find, that is the truth about your app, not whatever the marketing page says.

PUBLISHING: THE HOME-SCREEN APP

What you publish is a web app with a link. On a phone the user adds it to their home screen and it then opens like an installed app, full screen, with an icon.

For almost every internal tool this is better than an app store: it installs in two taps, costs nothing, and every update reaches everybody immediately with no review. Set a sensible name and icon, and show users how to add it - most have never done it and will not work it out alone.

THE TEST THAT DECIDES WHETHER PEOPLE USE IT

Before you hand anything over, open it on the cheapest Android phone you can find, on mobile data, from a cold start. Watch how long the first useful screen takes. Scroll the longest list. Note the data used.

A tool that is pleasant on a laptop over fibre and unusable on a 15,000-shilling phone on a daily bundle has not been built for the people who will use it.
lessons.practice:
Build one real internal tool, make it genuinely private, and test it where it will be used.

Step 1. Pick a real small need: a stock list, a visit log, a repair tracker, a class attendance register. Write the one sentence from lesson 1.

Step 2. Build the tables before any screen. For each table write the fields, the unique id column, and which values must NOT be duplicated anywhere else.

Step 3. Create one relation, one lookup and one rollup. Write what each one does in your app - for example, each order points to its customer, the order screen shows the customer's phone, and the customer screen shows their total number of orders.

Step 4. Replace one stored calculation with a computed column. Then write one line on where that computation runs and whether anything outside the app can see the result.

Step 5. Make it private properly. Mark an owner column on the table holding personal data, and set up roles for at least two kinds of user.

Step 6. Now break in deliberately. Create a second test account, sign in as that user, and try to see the first user's rows. Write down what you could and could not see. If you could see anything you should not, fix the owner column and test again. Also write down who else can open the underlying spreadsheet.

Step 7. Work out your row runway:

- Row limit of your current tier: ____
- Expected new rows per month: ____
- Months until you hit it: ____
- What the documentation says happens at the limit: ____

Step 8. Test offline honestly. Open the app with no connection from a cold start, add a record, reconnect, and write down exactly what happened.

Step 9. Publish it, set the name and icon, and add it to a phone's home screen yourself. Then run the real test: cheapest Android phone you can borrow, mobile data, cold start. Record seconds to first useful screen, scrolling smoothness on your longest list, and data used. Write one change you will make because of what you saw.

Step 10. If the app holds personal data, write one line naming what you will confirm with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner before real data goes in.

quiz.question: Your app filters a list so each user sees only their own orders. Is that data private?
options: Yes, because the filter hides other rows
Yes, because users must log in first
No - a filter is a display choice; privacy requires marking an owner column so other rows are never sent to the device
No, because spreadsheet-backed apps cannot hold private data at all

quiz.question: A customer's phone number is needed on every order screen. What is the right way to do it?
options: Type the phone number into each order row
Create a relation from order to customer and use a lookup to display the number, so it is stored once
Keep a second sheet of phone numbers copied across nightly
Store it in a computed column on the order table

lessons.title: Building an App in Adalo
objectives: Build on a platform with its own database: collections, relationships, and lists driven by the logged-in user
Decide honestly whether your app needs to be in an app store, and account for the fees, the review and the rejection risk before promising it
Recognise where this class of tool slows down, and design lists and screens so it does not
lessons.notes:
This class of builder gives you its own database rather than sitting on a spreadsheet, plus screens that behave more like a conventional mobile app and the option to publish to the app stores. The trade is that your data now lives inside the vendor, where you cannot open it in a sheet.

COLLECTIONS AND RELATIONSHIPS

A collection is a table. A property is a field. The modelling rules from lesson 1 apply unchanged, and the relationship between collections is the part worth care.

Think in sentences and then build what the sentence says:

- "A booking belongs to one customer, and a customer has many bookings."
- "A product belongs to one category; a category has many products."
- "A user can save many listings, and a listing can be saved by many users."

That last one is different in kind - many on both sides - and it needs its own joining collection or the platform's many-to-many option. Trying to force it into a single field is a common early mistake and it will not scale past the first demo.

THE LOGGED-IN USER IS THE MOST USEFUL IDEA HERE

Almost every screen in a real app is "the things belonging to whoever is signed in". These platforms give you a way to refer to the current user directly, and you use it constantly:

- Filter a list to records linked to the current user.
- Show or hide a button depending on who is looking.
- Link a new record to the current user automatically when it is created, rather than asking them to choose themselves from a dropdown.

That last one is worth stating plainly: never make a user select their own name from a list to file their own record. It is slower, it leaks everybody's names, and they will pick the wrong one.

And the same warning as the previous lesson applies, because it is the error that recurs on every platform: FILTERING A LIST IS NOT SECURITY. Check how your platform enforces access on the data itself, test from a second account, and never conclude that data is protected because the screen does not display it.

ACTIONS: WHAT BUTTONS DO

A button runs a list of actions in order: create a record, update a record, link records, navigate, send a notification, call an external service.

Two disciplines keep this maintainable:

- KEEP ACTION CHAINS SHORT. When a button needs nine conditional steps, the logic has outgrown the visual editor and you are building something nobody will be able to change later - including you.
- MAKE DESTRUCTIVE ACTIONS CONFIRM. A delete button with no confirmation step will delete real data, because people tap by accident on phones.

External service calls are how you escape the platform's limits - sending an SMS, triggering a payment, pushing a row to a sheet. Note that this is usually a paid-tier feature, so check that before designing around it.

THE APP STORE QUESTION, ANSWERED HONESTLY

This is the main reason people choose this class of tool, so be precise about what it involves.

THE COSTS, before your subscription:

- An Apple developer account is an annual fee, in dollars, renewed every year or your app leaves the store.
- A Google Play developer account is a one-off fee, much smaller.
- Both need a payment card that works internationally, and identity verification. Google in particular has tightened developer verification requirements, and for an organisation account the paperwork is real.

THE REVIEW, and the rejection you should expect:

Apple's guidelines require an app to provide meaningful functionality of its own. An app that is essentially a wrapper around a website, or that duplicates what a web page already does, is routinely rejected under the minimum-functionality rule. This catches a lot of no-code apps, because a simple directory or form-filling app genuinely is close to being a web page.

Also expect to be asked for: a privacy policy at a public URL, accurate declarations of what data you collect, working test credentials for the reviewer, and a reason your app needs each permission it requests. Missing any of those is a rejection, not a question.

THE RELEASE CYCLE. After launch, every change goes through review again. A typo fix is a submission. Plan for days, not minutes, and keep a web version for anything that must be fixed immediately.

SO WHEN IS A STORE LISTING WORTH IT?

- Worth it when the app must be discoverable by strangers searching a store, when it genuinely needs native features, or when the client's credibility depends on being there.
- NOT worth it for an internal tool used by known staff. A web app on the home screen does the job, updates instantly, costs nothing extra, and cannot be rejected by anybody.

Decide this before you quote, because the fees, the delay and the rejection risk all belong in the price.

PUSH NOTIFICATIONS

Often the real reason a client wants a store app. Worth knowing two things: they generally require the installed app rather than the web version, and they are easy to overuse. An app that notifies people about things they did not ask about gets uninstalled, and an uninstalled app sends no notifications at all.

WHERE THIS CLASS OF TOOL GETS SLOW

Performance is the commonest complaint, and it is usually caused by the same three things:

- LONG LISTS loading everything at once. Limit how many items a list fetches, add search and filters, and paginate rather than scrolling a thousand rows.
- TOO MANY RELATIONSHIPS FOLLOWED ON ONE SCREEN. Each one is more data to fetch. Show a summary and let the user tap through for detail.
- FULL-SIZE IMAGES. An uploaded photo straight from a phone camera is several megabytes. Resize before upload. This is the single biggest cause of an app that is slow and expensive for users on metered data.

Design for the phone your users have. Then verify it on that phone, on mobile data, from a cold start - the same test as every other lesson in this course, because it is the test that predicts whether anybody keeps using what you built.
lessons.practice:
Build an app with real users and real relationships, and settle the app-store question with numbers.

Step 1. Model it as sentences. Write at least three relationship sentences for your app, and mark which if any are many-to-many. For those, write how you will structure the joining collection.

Step 2. Build the collections and relationships. Then create a list screen filtered to the logged-in user, and confirm it shows only that user's records.

Step 3. Fix the self-selection anti-pattern. Make a create-record action that links the new record to the current user automatically. Confirm no dropdown of other people's names appears anywhere.

Step 4. Test access from a second account, as in the previous lesson. Sign in as a different user and try to reach the first user's data. Write what you found and how the platform actually enforces it.

Step 5. Add one action chain with a confirmation step on a destructive action. Count the steps in your longest chain. If it is more than about five, write one sentence on how you would simplify it.

Step 6. Answer the store question with arithmetic:

- Does this app need to be discoverable by strangers in a store? Yes or no, with a reason.
- Apple annual developer fee in shillings: ____
- Google one-off developer fee in shillings: ____
- Days you would allow for first review, and for each later update: ____
- Your honest assessment of minimum-functionality rejection risk, in one sentence: ____

If the answer to the first question was no, write the sentence you will say to the client about publishing a home-screen web app instead.

Step 7. If you are going to the stores, prepare the four things that cause rejections: a privacy policy at a public URL, accurate data-collection declarations, working test credentials for the reviewer, and a reason for each permission. Write down the status of each.

Step 8. Make it fast. Limit your longest list to a page of items, add a search field, and resize one image before upload - record the file size before and after.

Step 9. Run the cheap-phone test on mobile data from a cold start. Record time to first useful screen, scrolling on the longest list, and data used. Write one change you made because of it.

quiz.question: Your no-code app is largely a directory that a web page could already provide. What should you expect when submitting it to Apple's store?
options: Automatic approval, since no-code apps are exempt from review
A likely rejection under the minimum-functionality guideline, because it offers little beyond a website
Approval but no search visibility
A requirement to publish on Google Play first

quiz.question: A user files their own service request. How should the record be linked to them?
options: Ask them to pick their name from a dropdown of all users
Link it to the logged-in user automatically when the record is created
Have an administrator assign it afterwards
Store their name as free text they type in

lessons.title: Building in FlutterFlow
objectives: Explain why a code-generating builder is the answer to lock-in, and what responsibility that transfers to you
Set up a real backend with authentication, and write access rules that do not leave the database open to the world
Judge when this tool is the right choice and when it is more work than the project justifies
lessons.notes:
This is a different category from the previous two lessons. A code-generating builder gives you a visual editor over a real application framework and lets you EXPORT THE SOURCE CODE. That single capability changes the economics of everything lesson 1 said about lock-in.

WHY THAT MATTERS

With most no-code tools, the app lives in the vendor's account forever. Here, the project can be exported as a real codebase that a developer can open, change and build without the vendor existing at all.

Two caveats, stated plainly:

- Code export is generally a PAID-PLAN feature. If escaping lock-in is your reason for choosing the tool, confirm your plan actually includes export before you build on it.
- Exported code is generated code. A developer can work with it, but it will not look like what a careful human would have written, and somebody has to be willing to maintain it. "We can always export" is only an exit if a person exists at the other end.

WHAT YOU TAKE ON IN EXCHANGE

The previous two lessons hid real concepts from you. This one does not, and you have to learn them.

LAYOUT IS A TREE OF WIDGETS. Everything on screen is a component inside a component: a column containing rows containing text and images, with padding and alignment set at each level. Nothing is dragged to a free position. This is more rigid than a page designer and it is why the result adapts properly to different screen sizes.

STATE IS SOMETHING YOU MANAGE. A variable that belongs to one screen, or to the whole app, or to the current page's loaded data. A great many beginner bugs - a value that does not refresh, a counter that resets, a form that loses its content - are a misunderstanding of which kind of state something should be.

THE BACKEND IS A SEPARATE SERVICE. You connect a hosted database and authentication service rather than getting one bundled. Your data lives in YOUR backend account, which is good: even without code export, the data is already yours.

QUERIES ARE EXPLICIT AND THEY COST. You say which collection to read, with what filter and what limit. Those reads are billed by the backend, per document read. A screen that queries a whole collection every time it opens is both slow and a bill, and that is the commonest beginner mistake once an app has real users.

THE ONE THAT CAUSES REAL HARM: ACCESS RULES

Read this section twice. It is the single most consequential thing in the lesson.

A hosted database is protected by rules you write. During development, the tutorial-standard rule allows anybody to read and write everything, because it makes everything work immediately while you build.

If that rule reaches production, your entire database is readable and writable by anyone on the internet who finds the endpoint - and the endpoint is inside your published app, so finding it is trivial. This has leaked a great deal of real user data from apps whose developers assumed a login screen was protecting them. A login controls who gets a session; the RULES control what a session is allowed to touch.

Minimum discipline before anybody real uses your app:

- Deny everything by default, then allow only what is needed.
- Make a document readable only by the user it belongs to, by comparing the signed-in user's id to a field on the document.
- Never allow a client to write fields it should not control - a role field, a balance, an approval flag. Those belong to server-side logic.
- Test the rules from an unauthenticated context, not only from inside the app. The platform's rules simulator exists for exactly this.
- Check them again before every release, because a rule loosened to debug something has a way of staying loosened.

Also keep API keys and secrets out of the app itself. Anything shipped to a device can be read off that device; a secret in a published app is a published secret.

AUTHENTICATION, DONE PROPERLY

Email and password is the baseline, and phone-number sign-in is often a better fit for a Kenyan audience - but note that sending verification messages has a per-message cost and a configuration process, so price it.

Three details that matter: verify email addresses if you use them, handle the password-reset flow rather than leaving users stuck, and decide what an account can do before it is verified.

RELEASING, AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY COSTS IN TIME

You can publish a web version quickly. Store releases involve everything from the previous lesson - the developer accounts, the fees, the review, the privacy declarations - plus signing the app, which is its own small ceremony with keys you must not lose. A lost signing key for a published Android app is a genuinely painful problem.

Budget real time for the first release. Experienced people lose days to it, and a first-timer should assume a week and be pleasantly surprised.

WHEN THIS IS THE RIGHT CHOICE

- The app must go to the app stores and look native.
- A business will depend on it for years, so lock-in is unacceptable.
- You expect a developer to take it over and keep going.
- You need control over performance and layout that the simpler builders do not give.

WHEN IT IS THE WRONG CHOICE

- An internal tool for twelve staff. You will spend three times as long for no benefit they can see.
- A one-week turnaround. The learning curve is real.
- You will not maintain it, and nobody else will either. An app with unmaintained access rules is worse than no app.

THE HONEST SUMMARY

This class of tool is the bridge between no-code and software development. It gives you the exit that the other platforms do not, and in exchange it hands you the responsibilities that the other platforms were hiding - access rules above all. Take the bridge when the project needs it. Do not take it because it sounds more professional.
lessons.practice:
Build a small app with real authentication, then attack your own access rules until they hold.

Step 1. Confirm the exit exists before you build. On your plan, check and write down whether source-code export is included and what it produces. If it is not included, write what that means for your lock-in argument.

Step 2. Connect a backend and set up authentication. Choose email or phone sign-in and write the reason, including the per-message cost if you chose phone.

Step 3. Build two screens: a list of the signed-in user's records, and a form that creates one. Use an explicit query with a filter and a limit. Write the limit you chose and why.

Step 4. Now write real access rules. Start from deny-everything and add only:

- A user can read a document where the owner field equals their own id
- A user can create a document only with themselves as the owner
- Nobody can write the fields that must not be client-controlled - list them

Step 5. Attack your own rules. Using the platform's rules simulator, try each of these and record the result:

- Read another user's document while signed in as yourself
- Read any document with no authentication at all
- Write to a field you listed as protected
- Create a document with somebody else as the owner

Every one of those must fail. If any succeeds, fix the rule and run the whole set again.

Step 6. Count your reads. Open your list screen and work out how many documents one visit reads. Multiply by your expected daily visits and by thirty. Write the monthly read count, and check it against your backend's free quota.

Step 7. Check for secrets. Search your project for any API key or credential that will ship inside the app. Write down what you found and where you moved it to.

Step 8. Publish the web version and run the cheap-phone test on mobile data from a cold start, as in every other lesson. Record the numbers.

Step 9. Write the decision note you would give a client: three sentences on why this tool rather than a simpler builder, naming the exit and the extra time it cost. If you cannot justify it in three sentences, you probably should have used a simpler builder.

quiz.question: Your app has a login screen, and the backend rule still allows anybody to read and write all documents. What is the actual situation?
options: The data is safe, because users must log in to reach the screens
The whole database is readable and writable by anyone who finds the endpoint, which is inside your published app - the login controls sessions, the rules control access
Only the collections used by the login screen are exposed
The platform blocks unauthenticated access automatically in production

quiz.question: A client needs an internal tool for twelve staff, delivered next week. Why is a code-generating builder usually the wrong choice here?
options: It cannot connect to a database
It cannot publish a web version
The learning curve and release work cost far more time for no benefit those twelve users would notice
It does not support authentication

lessons.title: Turning No-Code Into Income
objectives: Choose between the three ways no-code earns - client builds, your own product, and internal tools inside a job - on the basis of what each actually requires
Price a build that includes the subscription problem, and put the client's account in the client's name from the first day
Write a scope that survives contact with a client, and handle deposits, handover and maintenance so the project ends cleanly
lessons.notes:
There are three ways this skill earns money, and they are different jobs.

1. BUILDING FOR CLIENTS. Somebody pays you to build their tool. Fastest to start, and the most common. Income is project-shaped: good months and empty months.

2. BUILDING YOUR OWN PRODUCT. You build something and charge users for it. Much harder, much slower, and it is a marketing business rather than a building one. Most no-code products earn nothing, for the same reason most courses and most affiliate sites earn nothing - no audience.

3. BUILDING INTERNAL TOOLS WHERE YOU ALREADY WORK. The most underrated. If you work anywhere with spreadsheets being emailed around, you can replace one with a working tool in a week. That is visible, valued, and the most reliable route to being paid more for the skill - and you keep a salary while learning.

For most people starting in Kenya, the realistic sequence is 3, then 1, and 2 only if an audience appears.

WHERE THE DEMAND ACTUALLY IS

Be specific, because this is where effort gets wasted. The work that exists is internal and unglamorous:

- Small businesses tracking stock, deliveries, debts and customers in a WhatsApp group and a notebook
- Schools recording attendance, fees and results on paper
- Clinics and pharmacies tracking inventory and patient visits
- Cooperatives and chamas recording contributions and loans
- NGOs collecting field data on forms that then have to be typed up
- Property agents and landlords tracking units, tenants and rent

Notice what these have in common. The customer already does the task, badly, and feels the pain daily. You are not persuading them a problem exists. That is a far easier sale than any consumer app.

A consumer app competing with free alternatives is a much harder business, and no-code makes building it cheap without making anybody want it.

PRICING A CLIENT BUILD

Price the OUTCOME, not your hours. A tool that saves a shop owner two hours a day is worth a great deal more than the three days it took you, and quoting hours invites a conversation about your hourly rate instead of about their problem.

Build the quote from these parts:

- DISCOVERY. A paid session to understand the problem and model the data. Small, but paid - unpaid discovery becomes unpaid consulting.
- THE BUILD. A fixed price for a fixed, written scope.
- TRAINING AND HANDOVER. Always included and always stated, because an untrained user will call you forever.
- MAINTENANCE. A separate monthly retainer, or an explicit statement that there is none. Decide before quoting.

Then add what the project really costs you: your own tooling subscription for the months it runs, your time in meetings, and the revisions you have already agreed to.

THE SUBSCRIPTION PROBLEM, AND THE RULE THAT PREVENTS IT

This is the single most important paragraph in the lesson.

NEVER HOST A CLIENT'S APP ON YOUR OWN PLATFORM ACCOUNT, PAID BY YOUR OWN CARD.

It feels helpful, because the client cannot easily pay a dollar subscription and you can. What it creates:

- You are personally liable for a monthly bill for an app you no longer work on.
- The client's business depends on your card not expiring and your account staying open.
- When the relationship ends, you are either paying forever or switching off a business's operations.
- You hold their customer data in your account, which is a data protection problem as well as an awkward one.

Do this instead:

- The account is created IN THE CLIENT'S NAME, with the client's email, paid by the client's card, from day one. You are added as a collaborator.
- If the client genuinely cannot pay in dollars, solve it openly: bill them the subscription in shillings plus a stated handling fee, in writing, as a separate line - and set a date by which they take the account over.
- Put the ownership in the written scope: who owns the account, who owns the data, what happens if payment stops.

Say the recurring cost out loud, early, in shillings per month. A client who learns about a permanent monthly fee after handover feels misled, and they are right to.

SCOPE, AND THE CREEP THAT EATS THE PROFIT

Write the scope before building and have the client agree to it. It should name:

- The tables and the fields
- Every screen, listed
- Who the users are and what each kind can see
- What it explicitly does NOT do - this list is the valuable one
- The number of revision rounds included
- What a change beyond scope costs

No-code attracts scope creep more than most work, precisely because changes look easy. "Can you just add..." is cheap to say and not always cheap to do. The answer is not no; it is "yes, that is a change - here is what it costs and what it does to the date". Written scope is what makes that sentence normal instead of confrontational.

GETTING PAID

- A DEPOSIT BEFORE STARTING. Half is standard. No deposit, no build. This single rule removes almost all bad clients.
- MILESTONES on anything longer than two weeks.
- THE BALANCE ON HANDOVER, and before you transfer full ownership of the account.
- IN WRITING, even for a small job - a one-page scope and a price, agreed by message, is enough to prevent most disputes.
- M-Pesa or bank transfer is simplest locally. Keep the record: date, client, amount, what for.

HANDOVER THAT DOES NOT HAUNT YOU

A project ends properly only when you have delivered:

- The account in the client's name, with their payment attached
- A short written guide - a page, not a manual - covering the tasks they will actually do
- A short screen recording walking through those tasks, which they will use more than the document
- The data model written down, so a future builder can understand it
- A stated end to your involvement, or a signed retainer

Without the last point, you have accidentally agreed to free lifetime support.

OBLIGATIONS THAT COME WITH OTHER PEOPLE'S DATA

If the app holds personal data - names, phone numbers, patient records, financial details - then you and the client both have duties under Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019: collect only what is needed, say why, keep it secure, and do not keep it forever. Health and children's data are treated as sensitive. Agree in writing who is responsible for what, and confirm current registration and compliance requirements with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner rather than assuming a small app is exempt.

And your own income is income. Keep a record from the first payment and confirm your position with KRA; the thresholds for the different regimes move, so check rather than assume.

THE FIRST THREE CLIENTS

They will come from people who already know you, exactly as in every other service business. The strongest opening is not an advert - it is building a small tool for a business you already use, showing the owner, and asking what it would be worth to them. Proof you can point at beats any description of what you could do.
lessons.practice:
Turn the skill into a priced, scoped, defensible offer.

Step 1. Choose your route: client builds, your own product, or internal tools where you work. Write the choice and one sentence of reasoning that refers to what you need in the next three months.

Step 2. Name three real organisations near you, by name, that currently track something important in a notebook, a spreadsheet or a WhatsApp group. For each, write the one task you would replace and what doing it badly currently costs them.

Step 3. Build the quote for one of them:

- Discovery session: KSh ____
- Build, fixed price: KSh ____
- Training and handover: included, stated
- Maintenance: KSh ____ a month, or explicitly none
- The platform subscription they will pay: KSh ____ a month, forever

Step 4. Write the subscription sentence you will say out loud at the first meeting, naming the monthly cost in shillings and who will own the account. Read it aloud. If it feels uncomfortable, that is exactly why it must be said early rather than late.

Step 5. Write the scope on one page: tables and fields, every screen listed, the kinds of user and what each sees, revision rounds included, cost of a change, and the DOES NOT DO list. Make the last list at least five items long.

Step 6. Write your payment terms in four lines: deposit, milestones, balance on handover, and the method. Then write the sentence you will use when a client asks you to start before the deposit.

Step 7. Prepare the handover pack as a checklist: account in client's name, one-page guide, short screen recording, data model written down, and a stated end to your involvement. Write the date you will do each.

Step 8. Build the proof. Make one small tool for a business you already use, for free, with a written limit on your time. Show the owner and ask one question: what would it be worth to you if this ran every day? Write down their answer. That number is your market research.

Step 9. If the app will hold personal data, write who is responsible for what between you and the client, and one line naming what you will confirm with the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner. Add one line on what you will confirm with KRA about your own income.

quiz.question: A client cannot easily pay a dollar subscription. What should you do?
options: Host their app on your own account and card, since it is easier

Create the account in the client's name with their payment from day one, and if they truly cannot pay in dollars, bill the subscription plus a stated handling fee in writing with a date for them to take it over
Use a free tier permanently and accept the vendor branding
Build it and let it lapse when payment fails

quiz.question: Which demand is the easiest to sell a no-code build into?
options: A consumer app competing with established free apps
A small business already tracking stock and debts in a notebook and a WhatsApp group
A social network for a new audience
A game
